docs.title: RoTab and Rosetta WebAssembly
docs.text:
RoTab is a Chromium new-tab extension for protein visualization and browser-based scientific computation. Selected Rosetta C++ methods are compiled to WebAssembly (WASM) and run in dedicated browser workers. The standalone library, @rotab/rosetta-wasm, exposes the same eight methods to other browser applications.

This reference describes RoTab 0.5.6, standalone adapter 0.1.0, and scientific source commit 369e400415dd5c585f80dcf7b647147ee520e8ba. Validation records identify the versions and artifact hashes tested. The latest packaged private pilot is 0.5.2; later interface updates have separate validation records.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Rosetta supplies the C++ scientific model, REF2015 energy evaluation, rotamer packing, minimization, FastRelax, and FastDesign. The WASM engine executes these compiled implementations.

The standalone adapter manages a dedicated worker, verifies engine and database identities, calls the compiled C ABI, and returns measured snapshots and final coordinates. It has no dependency on the extension's networking, storage, or UI.

RoTab adds the molecular viewer, energy history, shared-tab ownership, model checkpoints, and volunteer campaign coordination. Nostr provides discovery and signaling; WebRTC transfers jobs and results between browsers. The submitting browser coordinates each campaign.

docs.title: Browser execution
docs.text:
Calculations run in the browser. Participants do not need Docker, Node.js, Python, BOINC, a native companion, or a local task server. Standalone applications serve their JavaScript, WASM, and database assets over HTTP(S). Compilers and native reference tools are used separately for building and validation.

Independent Nostr relays support discovery. STUN and optional TURN infrastructure help browsers establish connections across networks. Network architecture describes these services and their limits.

docs.title: Scientific scope
docs.text:
The eight supported methods accept a single chain of standard amino acids in PDB format. Input admission has no residue-count cap, but each worker has a 512 MiB linear-memory ceiling. Supported chemistry and database coverage depend on the method and its validated fixtures.

Relaxation optimizes an existing structure. Its snapshots describe optimization states, not a time-resolved molecular-dynamics folding experiment. Rosetta relaxation reference.

RoTab does not implement official Rosetta@home workunit submission, project validation, or BOINC credit. The port is independent of endorsement by RosettaCommons, Rosetta@home, or BOINC. Rosetta's license is separate from the MIT application and adapter code.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:

docs.title: One computing owner, many views
docs.text:
An exclusive Web Lock selects the computing tab. Other RoTabs receive BroadcastChannel status/structure updates and send controls to that owner. They do not independently start duplicate pools. Ownership is released by the browser; late heartbeats never authorize another tab to steal a lock from a suspended owner.

The owner creates dedicated workers for independent seeded models. Each worker has its own Rosetta globals, RNG, Emscripten filesystem and heap. Completed models are persisted before batch finalization. Handover replays unfinished model seeds and retains completed outputs. The extension service worker performs bookkeeping rather than hosting long scientific execution.

docs.title: Scientific message flow
docs.text:
1. A bundled fixture, imported benchmark or signed campaign assignment supplies PDB text, protocol and seed.
  2. Admission checks the input, fixed protocol and exact source/engine/data identity.
  3. The worker loads the packaged engine and calls rosettatab_run_protocol asynchronously.
  4. C++ snapshot hooks report real coordinates and full-weight REF2015 energy from display-only copies.
  5. The owner updates the focused model's history, renderer and resource readings, then broadcasts changed data.
  6. A finished result is checked, hashed and durably recorded. Campaign outputs enter a signed delivery outbox.

The renderer can interpolate between measured structures for presentation. Those interpolation frames are not scientific samples. The energy chart retains measured values, including rises during optimization.

docs.title: Trust and storage boundaries
docs.text:
Input data is untrusted even when signed. Protocols are allowlisted and executable JS/WASM is packaged, not supplied by a job publisher. Signatures bind provenance and sender identity; they do not prove scientific correctness. Browser queue receipts establish matching durable delivery; independent scientific validation is a separate step.

The publisher is the campaign coordinator. Its IndexedDB copy is not replicated into a globally authoritative ledger. Browser storage can be cleared or evicted; experiment exports are necessary durable copies. Only the SDK's caller decides whether to retain frames/results: the SDK itself has no IndexedDB policy or autonomous uploads.

docs.text:
Component Accepts Produces Does not own Input preparation Original PDB/ENT or supported compressed input Prepared single-chain PDB, preparation report and original/prepared hashes Scientific scoring or silent arbitrary chemistry repair Scientific C++ harness PDB pointer, protocol ID, seed and intensity Measured snapshots and a final JSON result Peers, browser storage, user permissions WASM host Trusted engine assets and validated run request Worker messages, allocated-heap telemetry, result/error A globally authoritative project queue Session and model pool Accepted local/peer task and local resource preferences Model checkpoints, focused trajectory and completed outputs Relay discovery or arbitrary native execution Campaign coordinator Target, short description, independent model count and seeds Fenced leases, signed catalogs and result receipts Other volunteers' CPU settings WebRTC transport Signed application messages Ordered authenticated peer delivery Durable acceptance or proof of correct science Nostr rendezvous Signed public presence and encrypted offer/answer payloads Discovered participants and connection signals PDBs, scientific results or campaign storage React/Mol* view Session snapshots and local presentation state Molecular rendering, energy graph and user controls Execution checkpoints or interpolated scientific evidence

The two browser hosts deliberately have different lifetimes. The extension shares compiled WASM code within concurrent model pools; single-worker runs compile inside their disposable worker. Each model receives an isolated instance that terminates on completion. The standalone client retains one instance for sequential calls until cancellation, failure or close(). A first call on either host includes Rosetta's lazy initialization. Reusing an SDK client can avoid repeating that initialization; reopening an extension model currently cannot. docs.title: End-to-end calculation flow
docs.text:
1. The UI prepares an input and records its provenance. A local start creates a task; a network start verifies a signed assignment first.
  2. The exclusive Session owner persists the batch definition before launching a scientific worker. A linked tab renders the same session without launching a second pool.
  3. The pool supplies the pinned manifest identity, protocol, seed, prepared PDB and local duty budget. Cold starts are staged until an earlier worker emits its first real frame.
  4. The host initializes the WASM instance and virtual filesystem, then enters the fixed C ABI with a heap-backed input buffer.
  5. C++ emits actual coordinates and REF2015 scores. Session retains bounded measured frames; Mol* interpolates only for display. Progress is an estimate of protocol stages, not a time-to-completion prediction.
  6. The finished model is committed locally. Network work additionally enters a durable signed outbox and remains pending until the publisher's matching receipt arrives.

Further architecture: browser ownership and model execution, connection establishment, assignment and return protocol, and standalone hosting.

docs.title: Benchmarks and interpretation
docs.text: The benchmark record separates scientific correctness of the pinned port, comparison with an installed official application, and reproduction of assigned Rosetta@home workunits. Recorded results are available for the first two categories. Official workunit reproduction remains pending.

docs.title: 1. Same-source scientific correctness
docs.text:
The native harness and WASM harness use pinned source 369e400415dd5c585f80dcf7b647147ee520e8ba. Fixed-coordinate scores must agree within:

absolute difference ≤ max(0.001 REU, 0.00001 × |native score|)

For optimization/design, the returned WASM coordinates are independently rescored natively under the same reporting function. Native and WASM trajectories need not be identical. Differences in their final chosen models are not a substitute for rescoring the same returned coordinates.

Recorded 1L2Y measurement Value Native fixed-coordinate REF2015 32.33483681374909 REU WASM fixed-coordinate REF2015 32.33483681375084 REU Absolute fixed-score discrepancy approximately 1.75 × 10⁻¹² REU WASM FastRelax returned-coordinate energy −48.17565422427388 REU Native rescore of that returned structure −48.17565422424631 REU Absolute returned-score discrepancy approximately 2.76 × 10⁻¹¹ REU Eight-protocol measured peak allocated heap 278,396,928 bytes Scientific JS/WASM/database package 146,090,371 bytes

Recorded checks cover all eight engine methods against native Rosetta and standard Chrome and Brave virtual machines. Most fixtures use 20-residue 1L2Y, seed 17; FastDesign checks for the engine with large-input memory adaptations use its first eight residues in Node and browsers. The historical engine's full 20-residue FastDesign run took approximately 27 minutes and has separate recorded hashes in the evidence inventory. A separate 76-residue 1UBQ browser scoring check and the private 865-residue memory regression test larger inputs. These fixtures do not establish general input coverage, size scalability or reliable runtimes for new proteins.

docs.title: 2. Standalone SDK acceptance
docs.text:
The SDK acceptance script loads no extension in installed Chrome and Brave. Each browser performs real score, minimize and relax on 1L2Y, seed 17, at a 75% duty target. All six outputs require independent rescoring and input/output provenance checks, together with real snapshots, sequential warm worker reuse, mismatched-manifest rejection and wrong-asset-hash rejection. Every external request is blocked. A temporary loopback listener streams the single WASM asset for this developer test and closes afterward; no task server, container or participant helper is involved.

Standalone scientific browser coverage includes score, minimize and relax. Dispatch and contract checks cover all eight methods, with separate scientific evidence from the matching engine's eight-protocol tests. These records do not constitute an all-eight-method standalone browser benchmark. Exact SDK hashes, output records and measured values are in the evidence inventory.

The SDK adds asset hashing and uses a verified-byte instantiation hook. Its cold timing is not directly comparable to the extension's different worker host, and the two browsers were exercised concurrently during acceptance. Those timings are observations, not a controlled Chrome-versus-Brave performance ranking.

docs.title: 3. Installed official Beta versus browser reference
docs.text:
The installed Rosetta Beta 6.04 executable and browser WASM ran one-repeat FastRelax on the repository's same first 1L2Y model, seed 17. Returned structures were scored with one common pinned REF2015 reference.

Measurement Result Initial common score 32.334836814 REU Official executable's returned coordinates, common score −48.202634589 REU Browser returned coordinates, common score −48.175654224 REU Browser minus official common score +0.026980364 REU Aligned C-alpha RMSD 0.007551132 Å over 20 residues

The structures are close for this fixture. The official binary self-reports source 76e2f63f750b32d50338385a5e1d99ecb36da226, while WASM uses a different source/database baseline. Binary/source correspondence and native database parity were not independently attested. The native run used an x86_64 binary on arm64 macOS. It was network-denied and isolated from BOINC credentials and live task slots.

Native score-file and pose-table energies precede PDB rounding and differ from common returned-coordinate rescoring. The native process wall time was 14.818 s including startup and shutdown, and its BOINC CPU summary conflicted with wall time. These records do not support a valid native/browser speed ratio.

docs.title: 4. Parallelism, recovery and volunteer delivery
docs.text:
Historical extension 0.2.0 multicore checks defaulted to four workers on eight reported processors. Ten tabs retained one computation owner. Pause/resume and active-owner handover preserved completed outputs, IDs and seeds; unfinished models replayed. Two-worker FastRelax batches at 75% duty took 118.518 s in Chrome and 105.287 s in Brave. These are operation observations, not randomized equal-resource speedup trials. Seeds 17 and 18 produced identical final coordinates on that fixture.

Recorded aggregate allocated heap peaked at 695,992,320 bytes with three fully initialized models active after handover; that is not a measured four-model full-initialization peak. Browser/compiler/viewer/process memory is additional.

The 0.5.2 acceptance run verified the current one-worker default, staged initialization, pause/resume and ten-tab ownership transfer in Chrome and Brave. Each browser produced four minimization outputs and two FastRelax outputs; every returned structure passed native rescoring. Tests explicitly requested four workers and observed a maximum of two simultaneously active workers under staged startup. Maximum measured allocated WASM heap was 231,997,440 bytes per worker and 366,215,168 bytes in aggregate in each browser. Worker memory was released on pause and completion, and saved coordinate frames restored and replayed. These heap figures exclude browser/viewer/process memory. The runs overlapped other acceptance workloads and are not controlled performance comparisons. Build-specific multicore report.

Extension 0.5.1's direct-peer checks produced four real WASM score/minimize outputs across Chrome and Brave. Its Nostr tests used a public relay, three isolated profiles per browser, two volunteers and four minimization outputs per browser. All eight network outputs passed independent native rescoring; maximum discrepancy was approximately 1.77 × 10⁻¹¹ REU. Publisher profiles ran no scientific worker. All profiles shared one machine, so reachability between volunteers on different networks remains untested.

The shared-TURN 0.5.2 pilot completed a scientific campaign check through the supplied Metered Free-tier standard.relay.metered.ca relay. Chrome and Brave each used three isolated profiles and a real public Nostr relay; two volunteers returned four packaged-WASM minimization models per browser family. Relay-only policy was forced in the test harness, and selected candidates at both endpoints were TURN relays over TLS. All eight outputs passed independent native rescoring (maximum absolute discrepancy 1.77e-11 REU). The test used no manual TURN credential entry. All profiles still shared one computer; different-network field testing remains required. Scientific relay campaign report.

UI/transport tests also use synthetic worker fixtures to exercise failures and scheduling quickly. Those establish behavior, not scientific execution, and are not counted as Rosetta models in the scientific evidence.

The October 11 volunteer UX check separately returned four actual packaged WASM Score jobs in each installed browser family, distributed among the publisher and two volunteers (eight returned jobs total). It used an in-process Nostr transport fixture with actual signatures, NIP-44 and local WebRTC. No native scorer or listening service ran for this check. The report binds the tested runtime; this confirms execution and delivery, not new native equivalence or different-network reachability. Interface-only checks are separate from scientific acceptance.

docs.title: 5. October 11 recovery and low-intensity observations
docs.text:
The reliability report records six isolated profiles in each installed Chrome/Brave test, actual signatures/NIP-44/WebRTC, a rejecting relay fixture, five retained remote outboxes while the publisher was offline, publisher participation, and six received models after recovery. Scientific workers were deterministic fixtures. This tests transport/scheduling and durable return, not real scientific equivalence, cross-NAT routing or public-relay write acceptance.

The same report contains a failed/unfinished 10%-intensity actual-WASM recording probe: only an initial Score frame was captured before its timeout. The report's top-level passed flag refers to the combined reliability work and must not be interpreted as a successful nested recording/thermal measurement. Existing successful scientific SDK/protocol reports remain separate and identify their own inputs, budgets and hashes. The recovery report applies to its recorded runtime hash.

Comparative temperature, fan-speed, battery and wattage measurements across users' Macs are not available. Startup can recur per extension model and begins before the cooperative budget timer; a low target can also lengthen waits. Further resource measurements need to distinguish cold and warm startup, active work and sleeping time.

docs.title: 6. Official task replay remains pending
docs.text:
The saved October 8 local inventory contained no Rosetta workunits/results. Historical project-status observations recorded an empty queue at their stated timestamps; they are not a live availability guarantee. No approved browser task feed, scheduler allocation, official result upload or credit has been demonstrated.

A complete workunit comparison requires the original application/version, exact input files and logical mappings, flags, restraints, seed, budgets, and output contract. A PDB extracted from a task can support a separate coordinate experiment without reproducing the original job.

docs.title: Measurement design
docs.text:
Controlled performance measurements require a fixed dataset, multiple seeds and input sizes, and repeated paired trials. Download, compilation, first-call scientific setup, warm execution, rendering, and result transfer have separate timing scopes. Worker comparisons also require equal model counts, seeds, and resource policies.

The current records provide fixture-specific observations. They do not establish a general native/browser speed ratio, equal-resource speedup, or a thermal guarantee.

docs.title: BOINC, Rosetta@home and what was ported
docs.text: Rosetta's scientific C++ methods have been ported to WebAssembly. The BOINC client has not been ported. BOINC provides the surrounding volunteer-computing platform: it allocates work, downloads application and data files, manages execution, reports results and supports project validation and credit. Rosetta is the scientific application launched by BOINC. BOINC overview, native application API.

docs.title: BOINC reference environment
docs.text:
The arm64 macOS reference environment used for comparison contained BOINC 8.2.11, a Rosetta Beta 6.04 x86_64 scientific executable, its graphics executable and a 418,361,967-byte database ZIP. No downloaded Rosetta workunits or results were present, so the environment provided no assigned task for reproduction.

A reference experiment ran the installed scientific executable on the repository's 1L2Y fixture in isolated scratch storage with networking denied. The executable reported source 76e2f63f750b32d50338385a5e1d99ecb36da226, which differs from the browser port's pinned source. Retained evidence includes inputs, outputs, hashes, sanitized logs and a common-scorer comparison. This experiment compares an official executable against WASM on a reference structure; it does not reproduce an assigned Rosetta@home workunit. See benchmarks.

The capture utility, scripts/capture-boinc-task.py, preserves an already downloaded task's allowlisted metadata, files, mappings and hashes without controlling the BOINC client. It excludes account and authentication files and does not request new work or upload results. The browser importer can derive a supported coordinate benchmark from captured PDB data. That derived benchmark does not reproduce arbitrary original flags, constraints or application behavior.

On the project application page checked October 9, 2026, published families include Rosetta, Rosetta Beta, Rosetta Mini and VirtualBox-based Python projects. No browser/WASM platform is listed. The current listing is separate from locally retained older files. Official application list.

docs.title: What an official workunit contains
docs.text:
A BOINC job can reference multiple input and output files with logical names understood by the scientific application. Task metadata also identifies the application, arguments, deadlines and resource bounds. Per-application templates describe file mappings and output size limits. A ZIP is a container for some jobs, not a universal scientific workunit format. BOINC job templates, job submission and control.

The pinned Rosetta BOINC application includes archive extraction/file resolution and dispatches on run:protocol; work can involve sequence/fragments, structures, constraints, templates, ligands, symmetry definitions or scripts. It can emit silent structure records rather than just one PDB. The list of 19 source branches is documented in experimental modules. A source branch's presence does not establish that Rosetta@home currently sends that workload. Pinned minirosetta.cc.

Volunteer parallelism commonly distributes independent model attempts and sampling jobs. In RoTab, each attempt receives the complete supported input chain. Modeling a domain or segment requires a defined scientific protocol, boundary conditions and validation; cutting coordinates alone would not preserve interactions with omitted residues.

docs.title: Relationship to the native scientific application
docs.text:
The production coordinate harness calls upstream scientific classes directly. It does not call the BOINC scheduler, runtime supervisor, slot resolver or native shared-memory graphics. Separate research builds also link the upstream minirosetta scientific dispatcher and a smaller cyclic family, but those have their own unpassed browser/admission gates.

Official browser-client support would require project agreement on an application and platform identity, engine distribution rights, a reviewed input feed, exact protocol and file contracts, native/browser validation, safe result reporting and accepted project results. These contracts must also specify flags and database resources. The scope reference describes related development areas. Agreement on one REF2015 score does not establish these operational requirements.

docs.title: Standalone SDK measurements

Recovery retains completed models and replays unfinished seeds. It does not serialize a suspended minimizer, annealer, complete Pose, or RNG continuation. Closing the last RoTab stops browser computation.

One trajectory is single-threaded. Independent models can run in separate workers; there is no pthread/OpenMP/MPI, CUDA, or WebGPU scientific execution. RoTab does not provide hardware temperature, fan-speed, or component-wattage sensors.

docs.title: Connection setup architecture
docs.text: RoTab has a rendezvous layer and a scientific-data layer. Nostr discovers compatible sessions and carries connection signals; WebRTC carries signed application messages after a peer session is established. The submitting browser remains the coordinator. There is no publisher-operated task API in this default path, but public relays and optional connectivity services are still servers.

docs.title: Establishing a session
docs.text:
Browser A              Nostr relays                 Browser B
   │── signed presence ────┬──── signed presence ──────│
   │← compatible peer ─────┴──── compatible peer →────│
   │── encrypted offer ────────────────→──────────────│
   │←────────────── encrypted answer ─────────────────│
   │                 ICE / optional STUN or TURN      │
   └════════ authenticated WebRTC data channel ═══════┘
                     signed catalog / task / result
  1. The owner loads a persistent P-256 participant signing identity and a separate local Nostr key. A signed binding ties the discovery key to the participant identity.
  2. It subscribes to the selected room topic on up to three wss:// relays. Fresh profiles use rotab-pilot-v3, relay.damus.io and nos.lol.
  3. Public ephemeral presence kind 23370 advertises compatible engine/source/hashes, protocols, availability and bounded counts. Its application lifetime is 45 seconds. New public announcements are coalesced to at most one every ten seconds; direct updates can arrive sooner.
  4. Compatible peers establish a signed offer/answer exchange. Signal kind 23371 carries a NIP-44 v2 encrypted payload for its intended recipient. Duplicate/older offers and repeated answers are handled idempotently.
  5. Initial ICE gathering waits up to eight seconds. Candidates arriving later are sent as bounded encrypted connectivity updates (signaling payload version 2), tied to the current session. Updates arriving before their invitation/answer are held briefly; duplicates and obsolete sessions are discarded. Invitation payload version 1 and presence wire version 3 remain unchanged. Both devices need a build that supports late-candidate exchange.
  6. ICE finds a network route. The resulting data channel verifies signed application messages and the expected participant before accepting a catalog, assignment, renewal, result or receipt.

RoTab's event kinds and payloads are application-specific. NIP-01 supplies the event/relay foundation; NIP-44 specifies encrypted content. Neither defines RoTab's compute scheduler.

docs.title: Retry and diagnosis
docs.text:
Relay acceptance does not guarantee delivery to an online recipient. While a connection remains incomplete, the initiator repeats its signed invitation in a fresh encrypted Nostr event at the next maintenance tick after twelve seconds. A repeated invitation can trigger retransmission of the cached answer without creating another session or duplicating an assignment. Late candidate batches also retry. A fresh connection attempt replaces an unsuccessful session after sixty seconds; older answers cannot bind to the replacement.

Live devices distinguishes route gathering, waiting for a reply and connection checks. A visible peer is an observed presence, not proof of a usable transfer channel. Retry connections requests a new setup for disconnected peers and preserves working links, campaigns and saved results. The lower participant ID remains the initiator; an encrypted reconnect request handles retries initiated from the other device.

Pending checks remain a setup state rather than a confirmed failure. An actual ICE/transport failure can report whether STUN supplied an external candidate or TURN supplied a relay candidate; these observations do not independently prove a NAT/firewall cause. Download connection diagnostics exports current connection/gathering/ICE/transport state, candidate types, numeric ICE-server errors and public relay origins/status. Version 2 adds a built runtime filename and up to four previous attempts per observed peer, including replacement reason and the last confirmed failure state. This in-memory history clears on network reconfiguration, peer expiration or reload. Reports exclude candidate addresses, raw SDP, keys, participant identities, TURN credentials and protein/job data. Experiment-record export is a separate feature and can contain scientific data.

docs.title: Shared relay access and campaign authority
docs.text:
The shared-TURN 0.5.2 pilot supplies generated relay authentication once to profiles without configured TURN, while retaining custom settings and previous opt-outs. It uses turns:standard.relay.metered.ca:443?transport=tcp; the standard source build supplies no shared credentials. Participants do not need separate provider accounts. Access is extractable from the private distributable, and relayed traffic from all recipients consumes the operator account's allowance. Previously applied credentials are not automatically replaced on an upgrade.

Relay authentication is independent of campaign authority. Any compatible connected participant can publish a campaign and volunteer; the TURN account owner has no special sender role. Each publishing browser coordinates its own durable queue and must remain available for assignment and result receipts. There is no approved-sender allowlist, and a room topic does not restrict access.

The current provider allowance, monthly renewal, availability limits and service-change instructions are documented in the TURN usage guide. TURN carries encrypted transfers and does not execute scientific workers or replace Nostr signaling. Provider quota failure can leave discovery working while fallback data channels cannot connect.

docs.title: Failure isolation and queue responsiveness
docs.text:
ICE gathering and connection setup run outside the durable ledger's serialized operations. A pending offer for one peer must not block another peer's renewal, assignment or result. Per-link sends preserve order, but backpressure on one channel does not stall the global scheduler. Repeated in-flight commands are bounded/deduplicated.

The Nostr transport retains a bounded, short-lived outbox: at most 65 pending items, with newer presence replacing older presence. Unacknowledged sends retry after eight seconds while their 45-second lifetime remains valid. Rate-limited writes back off for 15 seconds; other rejections back off for 60 seconds. Relay-specific errors remain visible without converting every healthy relay/direct peer into a global failure. Closed subscriptions reconnect; authentication-required relays are reported rather than silently treated as usable. NIP-42 authentication is not implemented.

Existing direct sessions can remain usable during relay rejection. If no ICE route works, adding relays alone does not solve it: configure a suitable TURN service or test another network. Scientific payloads do not fall back to a public Nostr event.

docs.title: Manual pairing and evidence
docs.text:
Advanced Direct pairing / Peer collaboration exchanges signed RT1. invitation/reply codes manually. It is a separate one-peer workflow with one to four independent models per job. Both peers should verify fingerprints and retain identity when retrying old results. It uses the same pinned science rather than requiring a native helper.

Recorded transport checks exercised delayed candidates, missing setup signals, rejecting relay fixtures, offline completion, and publisher reload. Separate scientific campaigns used public relays and real WASM. All recorded multi-profile acceptance ran on one computer; different-network reachability and comparative thermal behavior remain outside those results. Validation summaries, benchmarks.

docs.title: Campaign, model, assignment and result
docs.text:
Object Meaning Durable owner Target Prepared PDB plus input/preparation hashes and provenance Publisher, then assigned workers Campaign Title, required description (up to 240 characters), protocol, model count and base seed Publisher campaign-ledger Model attempt One independent model index and its seed Publisher Lease Current worker, signed job, unique token and expiry Publisher; signed assignment retained by worker Progress Worker-reported state, fraction, elapsed time, snapshots and optional energy Publisher's current lease Result outbox entry Signed completed coordinates and provenance awaiting receipt Worker network-ledger Outcome/receipt Publisher's durable matching result and delivery acknowledgment Publisher; receipt retained by worker

One submitted protein can request 1 to 1,000 independent models with distinct sequential seeds. Each attempt receives the complete supported input chain. Independent models may converge to similar structures, and the number requested does not guarantee that many volunteers are available.

docs.title: Submission and admission
docs.text:
The submitting browser prepares the file locally, requires a short research description and chooses a fixed protocol. The coordinator saves the campaign before advertising it through signed direct catalogs. Public presence exposes counts/capabilities rather than the full protein or description. Also calculate on this browser defaults checked, so the sender can be a worker as well as coordinator.

A received assignment is untrusted input despite its signature. Admission verifies publisher/recipient identity, schema, prepared input hash, current engine/source/database hashes, method, seed and protocol budget. Peers cannot supply arbitrary scripts, command-line flags, plugins, a replacement WASM URL or a volunteer's CPU preferences.

docs.title: Scheduling algorithm
docs.text:
VolunteerNetwork.schedule() collects compatible connected participants and the eligible local participant. CampaignQueue.assign() serializes the durable decision:

  1. Build the set of workers with unexpired leases across campaigns.
  2. Skip duplicate, stale (30-second scheduler presence), unavailable, occupied or non-consenting workers.
  3. Scan active campaigns in stored order. Require matching scientific identity/protocol, a description and local participation permission for the publisher.
  4. Find an unfinished model whose lease is absent or expired. Create a new signed job identity and random lease token for that model's seed.
  5. Commit the ledger, then send the assignment. Each eligible browser gets at most one network model at a time.

A newly submitted campaign can wait about five seconds for already-observed automatic volunteers to finish their direct handshake before a fast local scorer consumes its small queue. This is not equal-share or hardware-weighted scheduling. A small four-model campaign cannot simultaneously occupy six devices; connection readiness, local work and saved consent also affect distribution. Fairness across many publishers and malicious identity resistance remain future work.

docs.title: Worker lifecycle and live feedback
docs.text:
publisher commits lease → worker verifies + retains assignment
        → acceptance renewal / "loading" acknowledgment
        → Session checkpoint → Rosetta worker → real snapshots
        → authenticated progress renewals
        → completed model committed → signed result outbox
        → publisher validates and commits outcome → signed receipt

The 120-second lease is renewed during accepted/running work. Acceptance acknowledgment stops repeated full-PDB assignment sends. Progress is throttled, tied to the worker/attempt/token and checked for nondecreasing elapsed time. The sender can distinguish assigned/loading/running, latest energy/snapshot count, stale updates and completed work. A heartbeat or reported energy is not independent proof that a scientific result is valid.

After completion, automatic network work rests for 30 seconds before the next assignment. Pause new tasks revokes acceptance of later work while allowing a current model to finish; pausing/stopping the calculation itself terminates its worker and uses model-boundary recovery.

docs.title: Expiry, reassignment and delayed results
docs.text:
Expiry makes a model eligible for reassignment. It does not by itself erase the current token. A delayed renewal or valid result can still succeed if the same worker/token remains authoritative and the campaign has not been cancelled or the lease released. This matters when the publisher was offline while a volunteer finished.

Reassignment creates a new job/token. The previous worker's output becomes obsolete, even if its signature and coordinates are well formed. It cannot overwrite the new attempt. Duplicate delivery of the same recorded output receives the same acknowledgment; a conflicting output for that already-recorded assignment is rejected. Cancelled campaigns reject late completion.

Explicit campaign removal deletes its input, attempts and saved campaign outcomes in one durable ledger update, including withdrawal of active leases. The UI confirms this deletion first. It does not remotely interrupt an already-running worker or erase a separate browser run record. A delayed authenticated result for an absent campaign receives an obsolete receipt, allowing its outbox to settle without restoring deleted campaign data. Up to 128 recent former worker IDs are retained as connection hints so a reloaded publisher can initiate that return handshake; no deleted coordinates/results are kept in those hints. Default queue removal still requires a finished/cancelled campaign; the explicit controller action authorizes active removal.

The worker commits its signed outbox before sending and retries after reconnection until it sees a matching receipt. The publisher commits the outcome before acknowledging it. These commit-before-send rules and token fencing support idempotent delivery despite reloads and duplicates; they do not make the browser network a globally transactional database.

docs.title: Result receipt and scientific validation
docs.text:
The publisher checks the signed envelope, current token, input/method/seed/engine provenance and returned structure contract. Its saved outcome is explicitly marked scientificValidation: "not-verified". A received receipt confirms durable matching delivery, not independent energy rescoring, malicious-worker detection or official Rosetta@home credit.

Native/WASM comparison reports provide scientific evidence for their recorded fixtures. They are separate from live result admission. No native scorer is installed on volunteers' computers. Replicated coordinator storage, consensus, redundant-result scientific validation, project-approved credit and automatic publisher takeover are not implemented.

docs.title: Recovery and inspection
docs.text:
Keep the publisher's RoTab available to issue work and receive results. If it closes, volunteers can retain completed outboxes; new assignments and receipts wait for the same publisher identity/database to return. Clearing the publisher's data loses its authoritative campaign ledger. Export campaign records and completed structures for a separate backup; relays cannot reconstruct them.

Relevant sources: campaign-queue.ts (durable ledger/fencing), volunteer-network.ts (discovery/dispatch/retries), peer-protocol.ts (signed message and input/result contracts), and session.ts (scientific execution). See connection architecture and user troubleshooting.

docs.title: Live view and energy history
docs.text:
The viewport receives measured PDB snapshots from Rosetta's initial/final states, FastRelax commands, minimizer derivative evaluations and accepted packing assignments. Display-only copies are scored with full-weight REF2015. FastRelax's ramped objective is not mixed into the graph. The view follows the focused model when several independent models run concurrently.

Internal snapshots have a nominal 200 ms throttle, not a guaranteed five-frame-per-second stream. Rosetta initialization, large individual operations and event-loop scheduling can produce longer gaps. The source counter is not a fixed physical time step; a minimizer callback can be a trial state rather than an accepted optimizer step. Energies may rise and a final rounded-coordinate score need not equal the lowest displayed intermediate energy.

Retained graph points select exact measured frames. Selecting a baseline enables a rigidly aligned comparison and matched C-alpha RMSD against another frame. The overlay is a display transform, not a modification of either saved structure. Pinned residue selection persists independently of hover. Inspection does not pause science.

Visible rendering is capped at 30 FPS; hidden/offscreen views stop continuous rendering. Automatic orbit defaults on, with a saved Rotate protein automatically checkbox in Computation settings and a matching viewport control. Reduced motion disables orbit/transition motion, selecting a residue pauses orbit for inspection, and WebGL loss has a static fallback. These presentation controls do not alter the algorithm or seed.

docs.title: Display frames are not checkpoints
docs.text:
Each model keeps up to 240 coordinate frames within an estimated 8 MiB budget, alongside a 2,000-sample energy window. Exports retain frame hashes. These are visualization records, not complete Rosetta execution state.

A restart checkpoint records the original input, protocol, model IDs/seeds and completed outputs. It does not serialize the minimizer's stack, annealer, full Pose state or RNG continuation. Pause/stop, tab discard or owner closure terminates unfinished workers. A surviving owner skips finished models and replays unfinished seeds. Closing the last RoTab stops all browser workers; recovery follows the saved continuation preference.

docs.title: Resource readings
docs.text:
The strip distinguishes approximate JavaScript heap for the viewing page from fresh allocated WASM linear memory in scientific workers. These scopes exclude parts of renderer/process/compiler/GPU overhead and are not total tab RAM. Partial, stale, or unavailable readings are omitted.

Portable browser APIs do not provide reliable per-component CPU temperature, fan speed, CPU/GPU wattage or physical-core ownership for this product. The default browser UI does not show empty hardware fields. The browser-reported logical-processor count is a scheduling hint and may be reduced for privacy or resource policy.

Extension local/imported batches default to one worker, adjustable in settings. Each worker handles a separate model with its own heap. One Rosetta trajectory is still single-threaded. The single-owner guarantee means one supervised pool, not necessarily one scientific worker. Each browser accepts at most one network model at once and rests for 30 seconds after completion. Hosted attempts and available campaign assignments can use fewer workers than the configured maximum.

The extension's per-worker duty target defaults to 10% and accepts values from 10% to 75% in the scientific ABI. Profiles using the earlier implicit half-core/25% setting migrate once; distinct custom choices remain saved. Use low-power defaults restores one worker/10%. The standalone SDK independently defaults to 25% when its caller omits the option.

The target is cooperative active-versus-sleep time, not a promise of total machine CPU percentage. Rosetta initialization precedes the budget timer, and long synchronous operations can run until a yield hook. Concurrent extension pools share compiled code; a single-worker run compiles inside its disposable worker. Each model receives a new instance, so setup can repeat beyond the first extension use. The SDK can retain a warm instance for sequential calls. Memory increases with concurrent workers; hardware temperature/fan comparisons across users remain unmeasured. Startup implementation and completion memory lifetime.

docs.title: Volunteer network
docs.text: The submitting browser is the campaign coordinator. It stores a target, discovers online volunteers, issues bounded model assignments and receives signed results. All scientific computation runs in the accepting browsers. Nostr relays carry discovery/signaling, while protein data and result envelopes travel through direct WebRTC data channels.

docs.title: Discovery infrastructure
docs.text:
The default room is rotab-pilot-v3, with wss://relay.damus.io and wss://nos.lol as the default relays. Discovery is enabled on a fresh installation; computation requires explicit volunteer consent. Connection settings support up to three secure relay URLs. These independent servers have their own availability and policies. The default discovery path does not use a publisher-operated test server.

RoTab uses signed NIP-01 events, with application-specific ephemeral presence kind 23370 and signal kind 23371. Presence expires after 45 seconds. It binds a persistent local Nostr key to the existing P-256 participant identity and announces bounded availability, engine/protocol and queue-count metadata. Connection signals are encrypted with NIP-44 v2 for the intended peer. This is an application protocol, not a standard Nostr compute-market protocol. NIP-01, NIP-44.

Room names are discovery topics, not access-control secrets. Relays can see public presence, keys, timing and connection metadata; they do not receive plaintext input proteins, result structures or research descriptions. A signed direct-browser catalog supplies campaign title, mandatory description, method and remaining counts after peers connect.

docs.title: Task lifecycle
docs.text:
upload / prepare / describe / choose protocol and model seeds
        ↓ durable publisher storage
campaign ready → presence → authenticated direct peer → signed catalog
        ↓ volunteer consent or persistent automatic opt-in
fenced assignment (one model, seed, input and engine hashes)
        ↓
WASM computation → durable signed result outbox
        ↓ reconnect/retry as needed
publisher validates envelope + current lease → durable result → receipt

The coordinator gives each independent model an attempt identity and seed. Leases expire after 120 seconds and are renewed for active work. Expiry permits reassignment; a delayed renewal/result can still succeed while its original token remains current. Reassignment replaces that token, fencing the old output. Storage must commit before assignments/results/receipts become visible. Duplicate matching deliveries are acknowledged without adding another accepted result; conflicting, superseded or cancelled attempts are rejected. Assignment state machine.

The current application wire version is 3. All participants must update together; the former default room migrates to rotab-pilot-v3, while custom rooms and an explicit network-off choice are retained.

The publisher is an eligible worker when Also calculate on this browser is checked (the submission default). Local assignments use the same fenced queue, signed results and receipt path. At most one network model runs per browser at a time. A short initial dispatch window lets already-online volunteers establish direct links before a fast local worker drains a small campaign.

Active workers report bounded state, fraction, snapshot count, elapsed time and optional energy in authenticated lease renewals. Updates are throttled and bound to the current worker/attempt/token; older elapsed-time telemetry cannot replace newer telemetry. The UI differentiates a lease assignment from actual running progress and labels stale updates. These reports travel directly, including local loopback, never as public Nostr events. Progress is worker-reported and is not independent scientific verification.

Consent is local. A one-model request does not authorize automatic future work. Start volunteering explicitly opts into future assignments; Pause new tasks stops new acceptance while preserving the active run. A publisher cannot change a volunteer's worker count, intensity or automatic preference. Preference changes announce availability without tearing down existing connections.

docs.title: Participant and result identity
docs.text:
Every browser profile has its own durable signing identity. A public fingerprint identifies the sender; it is not an account verified against a person's legal identity. Multiple tabs in one profile share the computational session and identity, while separate profiles/devices can be separate participants.

Signed assignments/results bind campaign/job/attempt IDs, input hash, method, seed, source commit, engine/database hashes and output provenance. Local keys and connection credentials are excluded from experiment exports. Clearing storage can destroy identity and pending records. There is no distributed identity recovery or Sybil-resistant reputation mechanism yet.

docs.title: Transport and reachability
docs.text:
WebRTC uses ICE to find a route. STUN helps peers discover reachable addresses; TURN can relay encrypted traffic when direct connectivity fails. Neither service performs Rosetta calculations. The standard source build includes STUN configuration. The shared pilot additionally includes generated access to an independent TURN provider. Direct reachability across all NAT/firewall combinations is not guaranteed. WebRTC peer connection documentation.

Manual signed RT1. offer/answer pairing remains available for advanced testing. It supports one peer connection and one to four independent models per direct job; the automatic campaign queue has a separate larger attempt budget. Re-pairing must preserve identity to retry old outbox results. Manual-pairing bounds should not be mistaken for automatic campaign limits.

Automatic setup exchanges candidates that arrive after the initial eight-second gathering window. Missed invitations/answers and late candidates retry without creating duplicate jobs. Connection checks, retry controls and redacted diagnostics are described in Connection setup architecture. These recovery mechanisms improve signaling reliability; they cannot supply a TURN route when no such service is configured.

Relay settings include a managed-service guide and Test TURN allocation preflight. The test uses the entered settings without applying them, closes its temporary connection and starts no calculation. A successful allocation is followed by saving settings and verifying a real peer/job exchange. Cross-network setup.

docs.title: Network counters
docs.text: Online counts reflect currently observed, compatible, unexpired participants in this room and reachable relays. Queue counts come from direct publisher catalogs. They are local observations, not globally complete network statistics. Relay partitions, blocked peers and offline publishers can hide work or users. There is no authoritative worldwide membership count.

docs.title: Failure boundaries
docs.text:
Completed local work survives reload through checkpoints/outboxes, and delivery retries on reconnection. An offline publisher cannot issue assignments or immediately receipt results. A lost publisher database is not reconstructed from relays: relays hold no campaign proteins/results. There is no replicated coordinator ownership, global consensus, blockchain, storage availability guarantee or automatic publisher takeover.

The recorded 0.5.1 Chrome/Brave tests used public Nostr signaling, three isolated profiles per browser and real WASM minimization. Eight returned models passed independent native rescoring. All profiles shared one computer; volunteer testing across different networks remains pending. Transport tests that use synthetic workers are listed separately from this scientific evidence in benchmarks.

docs.title: Computation ownership
docs.text:
Session in apps/extension/src/session.ts is the supervisor. The Manifest V3 background service worker can be suspended by Chromium, so it only performs install bookkeeping and helps locate/focus the computing tab. Scientific execution lives in dedicated workers owned by an open RoTab page.

An exclusive Web Lock elects one computing owner per browser profile. Linked tabs receive state through BroadcastChannel and send controls to the owner. A quiet or suspended owner is not replaced merely because a heartbeat is late: the browser must release the lock. Different devices/profiles have independent owners and signing identities.

The main tab's favicon reflects status; linked tabs retain a neutral Histidine outline. The Histidine beside the RoTab text reflects session status in both views. A linked tab offers Go to main tab for owner-only changes. Navigating between Simple and Dashboard is local to that tab. Choosing a preferred opening layout in Appearance controls future new tabs, rather than copying another tab's current navigation.

docs.title: Model pool
docs.text:
BrowserModelPool supervises independent models, not parallel parts of one trajectory. Each model has a task/seed, status, execution budget, history, retained structures and optional final result. A single-worker run compiles the engine inside that disposable worker. Concurrent pools share a compiled WebAssembly.Module; every worker still owns separate linear memory, filesystem, Rosetta globals and RNG state. The pool releases its module reference once all remaining models have launched, and on stop/completion. Worker message/error handlers and transient live readings are cleared when the corresponding worker ends. Saved structures and histories remain available.

Session owner ── checkpoint: input + protocol + model IDs/seeds
      │
      ├── shared compiled WASM module (concurrent pools only)
      ├── model worker A → snapshots → final result → terminate
      └── model worker B → snapshots → final result → terminate
      │
      └── commit completed model → update focused view → fill available slot

Local batches use the configured concurrency. Defaults are one worker at 10% cooperative intensity; older implicit half-core/25% profiles migrate once, while distinct custom settings remain. A network browser accepts at most one network model at once and rests for 30 seconds after a completed model. The publisher's Also calculate on this browser option participates through the same network queue.

Cold starts are staged until the first scientific snapshot proves an earlier instance completed expensive preparation. This reduces overlapping startup allocation. It does not cap memory for arbitrary inputs or make initialization fully cooperative.

docs.title: Checkpoint boundaries
docs.text:
Before execution, the batch's original input, protocol, model identities and seeds are durable. When a model finishes, its output is committed before the batch is considered complete. The latest 20 completed browser run records are retained. A resumed batch skips completed models and replays unfinished seeds.

Pause/stop, tab discard and owner closure terminate active workers. A checkpoint does not contain a suspended minimizer stack, RNG continuation or full annealer state. Retained intermediate PDBs are display records, not executable checkpoints. A paused run may therefore redo unfinished computation when resumed.

Only the computing tab registers a beforeunload warning, and only while an identified calculation is loading or running. The handler checks the live session before requesting confirmation. Canceling departure leaves workers and ownership intact; accepting it allows the normal pagehide cleanup and lock release. Linked tabs and inactive runs do not register the warning. The browser controls the dialog text and may suppress it without prior page interaction or during a forced shutdown.

Closing the final RoTab stops scientific execution. A surviving linked tab can become owner after lock release and recover the saved boundary. Saved automatic continuation controls whether recovered work resumes automatically. Browser storage loss/eviction is outside this recovery mechanism.

docs.title: Display pipeline
docs.text:
Scientific callbacks include PDB, energy, source, sequence, iteration and timestamp. The owner follows one identified model; the chart does not interleave unrelated models. Per model, history retains up to 2,000 energy samples and at most 240 coordinate frames within an estimated 8 MiB frame budget. Large structures may therefore have more energy samples than retained coordinate frames.

Broadcasts carry frame metadata and new/changed coordinate payloads. Clock-only updates do not retransmit every PDB. A newly linked viewer receives a full frame reset. UI broadcasts are capped at five per second; the internal snapshot throttle is nominally 200 ms and does not guarantee continuous callbacks during a long operation.

Mol* draws the molecule on a transparent canvas at up to 30 FPS. Hidden/offscreen viewers skip drawing. Automatic rotation defaults on and its Settings/viewport controls save the same preference. Reduced motion disables rotation; selecting a residue pauses it for inspection. Smooth coordinate interpolation changes presentation only, and never inserts synthetic energies into the graph.

docs.text:
